summary: This standards-track RFC describes diagnostics for Peer-to-Peer overlays. It extends the RELOAD base protocol to collect diagnostic information and defines useful connection and node status data, with usage scenarios and examples.

eli5.summary: Tools to check on a network of computers helping each other, so you can tell which one is slow or broken.

questions: how to diagnose a reload overlay
what are reload diagnostic error codes
subtitle: Ping-like and traceroute-like tools for finding sick peers in a RELOAD peer-to-peer overlay.

tldr.problem: Nodes in a peer-to-peer overlay can be disabled, congested or misrouting messages, and keep-alive checks between neighbors alone may not be enough for the operator to find and locate them.
tldr.mechanism: It extends the RELOAD Ping method and adds a new PathTrack method. Both carry a DiagnosticsRequest with flags that say which status data to return, such as congestion, routing table size or uptime.
tldr.outcome: An operator can ping a node, and if that fails, walk the path hop by hop with PathTrack to see where the fault lies. Access to the data is limited to nodes the overlay configuration authorizes.

today: RFC 7851 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2016. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of RELOAD overlay diagnostics. It builds on RFC 6940.

sections.title: Why Overlays Need Diagnostics
sections.content:
RFC 7851 defines diagnostics for Peer-to-Peer (P2P) overlays built on the RELOAD base protocol (RFC 6940). Overlays are resilient to failures, but some nodes may still malfunction: they may be disabled, congested, or misrouting messages. That can degrade the service the peers provide together or interrupt it.

Keep-alive algorithms that probe neighbors periodically can only detect disabled neighbors. The RFC argues this may not be enough for a service provider operating the overlay, and proposes a framework with periodic and on-demand methods. It is meant as a complement to keep-alive algorithms, not a replacement.

The RFC names three usage classes: automatic checks built into the overlay routing protocol, diagnostics to follow up on one user's complaint, and system-wide checks of the overlay's overall health (bandwidth use, problem links, abusive or malicious nodes).
sections.eli5: Some players in a big team game may be asleep, overloaded or sending the ball the wrong way. This RFC gives the coach tools to find out which ones.

sections.title: Ping-like and Traceroute-like Modes
sections.content:
The design is modeled on the familiar ping and traceroute pair: ping (RFC 792) checks connectivity, and traceroute localizes faults hop by hop. RELOAD diagnostics offer two matching tools.

  • A ping-like mode, made by extending the RELOAD Ping method so it can return diagnostic data from the destination node.
  • A traceroute-like mode, made by defining a new method called PathTrack that collects information iteratively along the path.

The suggested workflow is simple. When the overlay gets alarms about degraded or interrupted service, send a Ping. If the Ping fails, send a PathTrack to find where the fault lies.

The RFC warns that the data collected is not guaranteed to be related to the earlier failure, although the information from the nodes traversed may let the user or management system infer the problem. The extensions follow RELOAD's own message routing, transport and NAT traversal rules.
sections.eli5: It works like the two classic tools: one asks 'are you there?', the other follows the road step by step to see where it breaks.

sections.title: How Ping and PathTrack Work
sections.content:
For the extended Ping, a new RELOAD message extension named Diagnostic_Ping (type 0x2) carries a DiagnosticsRequest. The request is forwarded by intermediate peers and ended by the responsible peer, which returns a response. The extension is not critical: a peer that does not support it ignores the diagnostic part and treats the message as a normal ping, and the sender MUST accept a response without diagnostic information. The extension MUST NOT be used with any method other than Ping.

PathTrack works iteratively. The initiator A asks its neighbor B for the next hop toward a destination. B answers with the next-hop peer C plus optional diagnostic information about B. A then asks C directly (using direct response routing from RFC 7263, or symmetric routing), and repeats until it reaches the responsible peer D. When a PathTrackAns carries a next_hop equal to the responder's own node ID, the initiator MUST stop.

If every flag in the request is clear, PathTrack degrades to a RouteQuery that only checks that the peers on the path are alive. The RFC prefers one PathTrack message per hop over a RouteQuery followed by Fetch requests, because under high churn the path could change between the two. If successive calls return different paths, the results should be discarded and the request resent.
sections.eli5: Ping asks the far end directly. PathTrack asks the first helper 'who is next?', then asks that helper the same thing, and so on, collecting a note about each one.

sections.title: The Request and Response Structures
sections.content:
Both methods share two data structures. A DiagnosticsRequest holds expiration, timestamp_initiated, a 64-bit dMFlags field, ext_length and a list of extensions. Times are milliseconds since midnight Jan 1, 1970 UTC. The expiration MUST be between 1 and 600 seconds in the future, which is used to prevent replay attacks.

The dMFlags field selects the base information wanted. Zero means none; all ones means everything. Extended requests go in diagnostic_extensions_list, each with a kind code. Kinds 0xf000 to 0xfffe are reserved for overlay-specific diagnostics, and kinds 0x0000 to 0x003f MUST NOT appear in the list because flags already cover them more compactly.

A DiagnosticsResponse copies timestamp_initiated, adds timestamp_received, a hop_counter copied from the TTL field of the request's forwarding header, and the requested diagnostic_info_list. The RFC says the default starting TTL is 100 hops unless the overlay configuration overrides it. A PathTrack request carries a destination and a DiagnosticsRequest; its answer carries a next_hop and a DiagnosticsResponse. The message codes are path_track_req 0x27 and path_track_ans 0x28.

The initiator can compute one-way delay from the two timestamps, and overlay hops from the hop counter. For this the overlay MUST enforce time synchronization with a central time server, for example with NTP (RFC 5905). Single-hop measurements MUST use ordinary IP-layer ping instead.
sections.eli5: The question form has boxes to tick for what you want to know, plus an 'expires at' time so old questions cannot be reused. The answer form has the replies and when the question arrived.

sections.title: The Diagnostic Information You Can Ask For
sections.content:
Section 5.3 defines the base kinds that a peer can report. Examples:

  • STATUS_INFO: an 8-bit congestion level from 0x00 (zero load) to 0x0f (congestion). How congestion is measured is left to each overlay.
  • ROUTING_TABLE_SIZE: how many peers are in the routing table.
  • PROCESS_POWER, UPSTREAM_BANDWIDTH, DOWNSTREAM_BANDWIDTH: capacity figures in MIPS and kbit/s.
  • SOFTWARE_VERSION: a string naming the manufacturer, model, operating system and software version, useful for spotting a misbehaving software version.
  • MACHINE_UPTIME and APP_UPTIME: how long the system and the P2P application have been up, in seconds.
  • EWMA_BYTES_SENT and EWMA_BYTES_RCVD: exponentially weighted averages of bytes per second, with a suggested alpha of 0.8 recalculated every five seconds.
  • UNDERLAY_HOP, MEMORY_FOOTPRINT, DATASIZE_STORED, INSTANCES_STORED, MESSAGES_SENT_RCVD and BATTERY_STATUS.

The first and last bits of dMFlags are reserved, so up to 62 base items can be requested. The appendix sketches uses: a peer can check byte rates to infer whether a neighbor is acting as a media relay, use STATUS_INFO along a path to pick another route, or average Ping hop counts to tune its timeouts.
sections.eli5: It is like a health checkup card: how busy are you, how much do you carry, how long have you been awake, what model are you.

sections.title: Error Codes and Intermediate Peers
sections.content:
Intermediate peers keep forwarding by the overlay's routing rules, but they also watch for trouble and report it to the initiator with new error codes added to the RELOAD error response (message code 0xffff). The upstream node returns the error, which helps the initiator see where and what kind of failure occurred.

  • A peer MUST check the expiration and, if the message has expired, return 0x17 Error_Message_Expired and discard it.
  • On an ICMP Destination Unreachable it MUST return 0x15; on an ICMP Time Exceeded it MUST return 0x16.
  • If its upstream peer broke the routing rules it MUST return 0x18 and identify that peer; if the Via List shows a loop, 0x19; if the TTL has run out, 0x1a.

If a requester asks for information it is not authorized to see, the receiving peer MUST return error code 2, Error_Forbidden.
sections.eli5: When a helper along the path notices a problem, it sends back a note saying what went wrong, such as 'this took too long', 'we are going in circles' or 'you are not allowed to ask that'.

sections.title: Authorization and Security
sections.content:
Diagnostic data is only provided to authorized nodes. The default rule for a type of information is deny. Authorization works per diagnostic kind: the overlay configuration file lists, for each kind, the NodeIDs allowed to read it, using diagnostic-kind elements with an access-node subelement for each node. The receiver identifies the sender from the signature that every RELOAD message already carries. Letting an individual node set its own access list is left out of scope.

The RFC warns that diagnostics can help attackers analyze overlay information to attack key peers, and could fingerprint a peer and destroy its anonymity. Overlays where anonymity matters greatly may find diagnostics problematic or undesirable. The security considerations of RELOAD also apply.

Appendix B records a design the authors dropped: having every intermediate peer send its own response. An attacker could spoof a victim as the sender and trigger many replies to it, and it would break RELOAD's one-request, one-response pattern.
sections.eli5: Not everyone gets to see everyone's health card. A list says who may look, because the same information could help a bad player pick on someone.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has created two RELOAD registries, one for the diagnostics flags in dMFlags and one for diagnostic Kind IDs, both with Standards Action as the policy for new entries. Flag 0x2 is STATUS_INFO, with matching Kind ID 0x0001, and so on up to BATTERY_STATUS.

The document also adds the PathTrack message codes 0x27 and 0x28, the six error codes 0x15 to 0x1a, and the Diagnostic_Ping extension code 0x2. It registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:p2p:config-diagnostics. The overlay configuration file MUST declare that namespace as a mandatory extension to RELOAD.
sections.eli5: The numbers and names used by this RFC are written in official lists so that nobody else reuses them for something different.
